params.question: What is the critical structural boundary that distinguishes an in-situ skin lesion from an invasive carcinoma?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The stratum corneum is the outermost keratinised layer of the epidermis. It has no role in classifying invasion — the defining boundary is the basement membrane at the dermo-epidermal junction, composed of type IV collagen and laminin.

Correct. The basement membrane, composed of type IV collagen and laminin, is the structural barrier between epidermis and dermis. Tumour cells remaining above it means the disease is in situ; breaching it makes the tumour invasive.
The stratum basale is the deepest cell layer of the epidermis, not a structural boundary. In-situ carcinomas can extend through the stratum basale but remain confined above the basement membrane.

Dermal papillae are projections of the dermis into the epidermis that increase surface area for nutrient exchange. The boundary that defines invasion is the basement membrane, not the dermal architecture.

overallFeedback.feedback: The basement membrane at the dermo-epidermal junction is the critical boundary. A lesion confined above it is in situ; once tumour cells breach this membrane, invasion has occurred and metastatic potential may follow.

The basement membrane (type IV collagen and laminin) at the dermo-epidermal junction is the defining boundary. Remaining above it = in situ; breaching it = invasive. This concept applies to all three skin malignancies covered in this lecture.

interactions.label: In Bowen disease, dysplasia extends through the full thickness of the epidermis.

params.question: In Bowen disease, dysplasia extends through the full thickness of the epidermis. Why is it still classified as carcinoma in situ rather than invasive carcinoma?

answers.text: Because the dysplastic cells are confined to the basal layer only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That description fits actinic keratosis, where atypia is limited to the basal and lower spinous layers with the upper epidermis spared. In Bowen disease, full-thickness dysplasia is the hallmark feature.

answers.text: Because there is no evidence of TP53 mutation in Bowen disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bowen disease does involve TP53 mutations driven by cumulative UV damage. The in-situ classification depends on basement membrane integrity, not on which mutations are present.

Correct. Despite full-thickness epidermal dysplasia, Bowen disease is in situ because the basement membrane has not been breached. Once tumour cells cross this boundary, the lesion becomes invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

answers.text: Because the dermis shows no solar elastosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Solar elastosis (blue-grey amorphous dermal change) is often present beneath Bowen disease as direct evidence of cumulative UV damage. Its presence or absence does not determine whether a lesion is in situ or invasive.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bowen disease is carcinoma in situ because the basement membrane remains intact despite full-thickness epidermal dysplasia. Once tumour cells breach this membrane, the disease becomes invasive SCC with 5–10% metastatic risk.
The intact basement membrane is what keeps Bowen disease classified as in situ. This same boundary concept applies to all three major skin malignancies — BCC, SCC, and melanoma.

interactions.label: Basal cell carcinoma, despite being the most common malignant tumour in humans,

params.question: Basal cell carcinoma, despite being the most common malignant tumour in humans, almost never metastasises.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. BCC is indeed the most common malignant tumour in humans, yet it almost never metastasises. Its danger lies in local destruction, not distant spread — it burrows into surrounding tissue (rodent ulcer) but does not travel to lymph nodes or distant organs. This key distinction separates BCC management from SCC and melanoma.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. BCC accounts for roughly 75% of all skin cancers yet has virtually no metastatic potential. Its clinical danger lies in relentless local tissue destruction — hence the name 'rodent ulcer.' This sharply separates its behaviour from SCC (5–10% metastatic risk) and melanoma (high metastatic risk via both lymphatic and haematogenous routes).

interactions.label: A melanoma biopsy shows tumour cells confined to the epidermis with horizontal s

params.question: A melanoma biopsy shows tumour cells confined to the epidermis with horizontal spread and no dermal invasion. What does this growth pattern indicate about the tumour's metastatic potential?

answers.text: Metastasis is likely because malignant transformation has already occurred

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the cells are indeed malignant, metastatic potential in melanoma is not acquired until the vertical growth phase begins with invasion into the dermis. Horizontal spread alone (radial growth phase) does not confer the ability to metastasise.

answers.text: The tumour is in the radial growth phase and has not yet acquired metastatic potential

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Radial growth phase involves horizontal spread within the epidermis without dermal invasion. Metastatic capacity is acquired only when vertical growth phase begins — tumour cells invade downward into the dermis, and Breslow depth then becomes the single most important prognostic factor.

answers.text: This pattern excludes melanoma and indicates a dysplastic naevus instead

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Melanoma in radial growth phase is still melanoma — a malignant neoplasm with pleomorphic melanocytes and pagetoid spread. A dysplastic naevus shows architectural disorder and cytological atypia but lacks the features of frank malignancy. The two are distinct diagnoses.

answers.text: Breslow depth measurement confirms no risk because there is no dermal invasion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While Breslow depth cannot be meaningfully measured without dermal invasion, this does not mean there is no risk. Recognising radial growth phase is itself critical because transition to vertical phase — with dermal invasion and measurable Breslow depth — can occur at any time.

overallFeedback.feedback: This pattern describes radial growth phase melanoma — horizontal spread confined to the epidermis, with no metastatic capacity yet acquired. Metastatic potential develops only when the tumour enters the vertical growth phase and invades the dermis.

Radial growth phase melanoma spreads horizontally within the epidermis without metastatic capacity. The critical transition is to vertical growth phase, where dermal invasion begins and Breslow depth — measured from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell — becomes the key prognostic factor.

interactions.label: A histological section shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading

params.question: A histological section shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a retraction cleft separating the tumour nests from the surrounding stroma. Which skin tumour does this pattern identify?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SCC is characterised by keratin pearls (concentric whorls of keratinised cells) and intercellular bridges, reflecting squamous differentiation. Peripheral palisading is not a feature of SCC.
Melanoma is identified by pagetoid spread of pleomorphic melanocytes and loss of maturation with depth. Palisading of basaloid cells is specific to basal cell carcinoma, not melanoma.

Correct. Peripheral palisading — basaloid cells arranged like a picket fence at each tumour nest's edge — and a stromal retraction cleft are the two diagnostic hallmarks of BCC. These features are not seen in SCC, melanoma, or dermatofibroma.

Dermatofibroma shows storiform (cartwheel-pattern) spindle cells with trapped collagen at its periphery. Clinically, it dimples inward on lateral compression (Fitzpatrick's sign). Palisading nests with retraction clefts point to BCC.

overallFeedback.feedback: Peripheral palisading and stromal retraction cleft are the defining histological features of basal cell carcinoma. For SCC, look for keratin pearls and intercellular bridges; for melanoma, pagetoid spread of pleomorphic melanocytes.

Peripheral palisading and the retraction cleft clinch the diagnosis of BCC. Remember the three histological anchors: palisading + cleft = BCC, keratin pearls + intercellular bridges = SCC, pagetoid melanocytes + loss of maturation = melanoma.
